title: Number of Islands
directAnswer: Treat the grid as a graph where adjacent land cells ('1') are connected. Scan every cell; when you hit unvisited land, run a flood fill (DFS or BFS) that sinks the entire connected island, then increment a counter. Each cell is visited once → O(rows × cols) time. Union-Find is an alternative when islands merge dynamically.

remember.pattern: Connected-components on a grid via flood fill (DFS/BFS)
remember.formula:
count = 0
for each cell (r, c):
    if grid[r][c] == '1':
        count += 1
        flood_fill(r, c)   # sink this whole island
return count

flood_fill sinks '1'→'0' and recurses/queues 4 neighbours.
rules: Each new unvisited land cell starts **one** island; the flood fill consumes the rest of it so it isn't recounted.
Mark visited by **sinking** the cell ('1' → '0') or using a separate visited set — never revisit, or you'll loop forever / over-count.
Explore exactly **4 directions** (up/down/left/right) unless the problem says diagonals connect.
DFS is simplest to write (recursion); BFS (queue) avoids deep-recursion stack overflow on huge grids.
Bounds-check before recursing: `0 ≤ r < rows` and `0 ≤ c < cols`.
whenToUse: Counting connected regions / blobs in a grid or matrix
Any implicit graph where neighbours are grid-adjacency
Detecting reachable clusters from arbitrary starting cells
antiSignals: Edges added incrementally and you must re-query connectivity → Union-Find shines
You need shortest distance between cells → BFS specifically (not DFS)
Weighted movement costs → Dijkstra, not plain flood fill
remember.takeaway: Number of Islands is the canonical grid-as-graph problem: every cell is a node, adjacency is the edge, and counting islands is counting connected components. Master the flood-fill template (DFS or BFS) and you've unlocked Max Area of Island, Surrounded Regions, Pacific Atlantic, and Rotting Oranges.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise a grid as an implicit graph and count connected components with flood fill, and whether you correctly mark cells visited so nothing is double-counted.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting to mark cells visited (infinite recursion / re-counting), going out of bounds, or counting each land cell instead of each connected component.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the grid-as-graph framing, give both DFS and BFS (and why BFS avoids stack overflow), mention Union-Find for dynamic connectivity, and note the in-place 'sink the island' trick saves the visited set.

problemStatement:
Given an `m x n` 2D binary grid `grid` which represents a map of `'1'`s (land) and `'0'`s (water), return **the number of islands**.

An **island** is surrounded by water and is formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically. You may assume all four edges of the grid are surrounded by water.
understanding: Count maximal blobs of horizontally/vertically connected land. Diagonal touches do NOT connect. We don't care about island size — just how many distinct connected groups of '1's exist.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do diagonal cells count as connected?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — only the 4 orthogonal neighbours (up/down/left/right) connect. I'd confirm, since some variants use 8-directional.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Am I allowed to modify the input grid?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If yes, I can sink visited land in place ('1'→'0') and skip a separate visited set. If the grid must be preserved, I'll keep a visited matrix.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can the grid get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 300×300 = 90,000 cells. DFS recursion could approach that depth, so for safety I'd consider iterative BFS to avoid stack overflow.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the cells characters '0'/'1' or integers?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Per the prompt they're the characters '0' and '1' — I'll compare against char literals, not ints.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Flood fill (DFS/BFS) is the default; Union-Find for dynamic edge additions.

approaches.name: DFS Flood Fill
approaches.whenToMention: The simplest and most common answer. Phrase it as 'when I find new land, sink the whole island recursively, then count one'.
hints: Think of the grid as a graph: each land cell is a node connected to its 4 land neighbours. How do you count connected components of a graph?
Scan every cell. The first time you touch an unvisited land cell, that's a brand-new island — bump the counter.
Then 'sink' the entire island so you never count it again: recursively turn this cell and all connected land into water (or mark visited), exploring the 4 neighbours.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Every cell is examined a constant number of times: once by the outer scan and once when sunk by a flood fill. So O(m × n). The recursion depth can reach the size of one island, up to O(m × n) in the worst case (a grid that's all land).
approaches.explanation:
Frame the grid as an implicit graph and count its connected components.

**Outer scan = component discovery.** Walk every cell. When you encounter land that hasn't been claimed yet, you've found the seed of a new island, so increment the count. The key is that you only count at the *seed* — the flood fill then absorbs the rest of that island so its other cells never trigger another count.

**Flood fill = sink the component.** From the seed, recurse to the 4 orthogonal neighbours, sinking each land cell to water (`'1'` → `'0'`) as you go. Sinking doubles as the visited marker: a cell that's already water is ignored, which is exactly the base case that stops recursion. The recursion naturally traces the whole connected blob.

**Why sinking in place is elegant.** Instead of a separate `visited[][]` matrix, mutating the grid records progress for free. State up front that this mutates the input; if the caller needs the grid intact, use a visited set instead.

**Base cases that keep it correct.** The recursion returns immediately when (a) the index is out of bounds, or (b) the cell is water. Those two checks prevent both array-index errors and infinite loops, and they're the only guards you need.
approaches.insight: Counting islands is counting connected components, and the increment happens exactly once per component — at the first cell the outer loop reaches. The flood fill's job isn't to count; it's to *erase* the component so the outer loop's counter stays honest.

approaches.name: BFS Flood Fill
approaches.whenToMention: Offer when grids are large enough to risk recursion-stack overflow. Same complexity, iterative queue instead of the call stack.
hints: Same idea as DFS, but explore the island level by level using an explicit queue instead of recursion.
When you find new land, mark it visited, enqueue it, and then repeatedly dequeue a cell and enqueue its unvisited land neighbours.
Mark cells visited at ENQUEUE time, not dequeue time, so a cell is never added to the queue twice.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each cell enters and leaves the queue at most once → O(m × n). The queue holds at most a 'frontier' of the island; for a grid that's O(min(m, n)) in the typical worst case (a diagonal frontier).
approaches.explanation:
Identical strategy to DFS — count once per component, then consume the component — but the traversal is iterative.

**Why iterative matters.** A recursive DFS on a fully-land 300×300 grid can recurse ~90,000 deep and blow the call stack in languages with modest stack limits. BFS moves that frontier into a heap-allocated queue, which scales to any grid size without stack risk.

**Mark visited at enqueue, not dequeue.** The single most important BFS detail: the moment you put a cell on the queue, sink it (or mark visited). If you wait until you dequeue it, the same cell can be enqueued multiple times by different neighbours, inflating the queue and re-processing cells. Enqueue-time marking guarantees each cell is touched once.

**Frontier expansion.** Pop a cell, look at its 4 neighbours, and enqueue every neighbour that's in-bounds and still land. The island is exhausted when the queue empties; then the outer scan continues looking for the next seed.
approaches.insight: DFS and BFS here are interchangeable for *counting* — both just need to fully consume each component. BFS is the safer default at scale because its memory is the frontier size, not the recursion depth, which can be far smaller and never risks a stack overflow.

commonMistakes: Not marking cells visited (sink or visited set) — infinite loops and over-counting.
Counting individual land cells rather than connected components.
Connecting diagonals when only orthogonal adjacency is allowed.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting to mark visited
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Without sinking the cell (or a visited set), neighbours keep re-entering the same land, causing infinite recursion/looping and counting one island many times.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Counting cells instead of components
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Incrementing the counter inside the flood fill (per land cell) reports the number of land cells, not islands. The count must happen once per seed, in the outer scan.
